source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology (Nature 566)
finding: Founding disruption-by-team-size study. Across papers, patents and GitHub software, disruption falls steadily as team size rises, while raw impact rises slightly. Small teams disrupt; large teams develop.
numbers: Data: more than 50 million works. Web of Science 43M articles 1900-2014 with 615M citations; USPTO patents 2002-2014; GitHub projects. From 1 to 50 members, disruption falls 70% (papers), 30% (patents), 50% (software).
quote: Disruption of these products dramatically and monotonically declines with each additional team member
limits: Observational. Disruption (CD index) is a citation-based proxy. Exceptions: fields that publish in conference proceedings (engineering, computer science), which WoS journal data miss.
agent_relevance: Background for design choice: adding workers raises output of the known kind but lowers the chance of a new direction.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology (Nature 566)
finding: Solo authors match five-person teams on hit rate but are more often highly disruptive. Large teams get more hits but of the developing kind.
numbers: Solo author as likely as a 5-member team to write a top-5% cited paper, but 72% more likely to write a top-5% disruptive paper. 10-person teams are 50% more likely to score a top-5% cited hit and are rarely among the most disruptive.
limits: Top-5% thresholds are arbitrary; correlational.
agent_relevance: Impact and novelty trade off along the team-size axis; a scaffold that wants novelty should not default to many parallel workers.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology (Nature 566)
finding: Effect is partly sorting, partly within-person. Comparing the same author across their own papers keeps about two thirds of the effect; one third appears only across different scientists.
numbers: About two thirds of the effect remains within author, with about 100 topic-position controls from title and abstract embeddings. Pattern holds in all eras and about 90% of disciplines; also holds when reviews are excluded.
limits: Topic controls improved model fit by an order of magnitude, so topic matters a lot. Not a randomised design.
agent_relevance: Team size has some causal pull on novelty, but task type confounds it. Test any team-size claim on matched tasks.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology (Nature 566)
finding: Mechanism: small teams search older, less popular work; large teams build on recent high-impact work and get cited faster.
numbers: Sleeping Beauty Index of solo and two-person teams is four times that of ten-person teams. Combination of distant journals peaks at 8-10 members and then falls below solo level at larger sizes.
limits: Search depth measured as mean relative age of cited references; popularity as median citations of references.
agent_relevance: Maps onto retrieval policy: large parallel samples cluster on recent popular answers; a minority should search old or obscure sources.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology (Nature 566)
finding: Funding does not rescue small-team disruption: funded small teams look like large teams.
numbers: Papers 2008-2012 acknowledging top agencies: small funded teams indistinguishable from large teams in tendency to develop rather than disrupt (Fig S30).
limits: Suggests review conservatism or lock-in to proposals; mechanism untested.
agent_relevance: Commitment to a fixed plan may reduce exploratory behaviour; do not freeze a plan too early.

source: Petersen (2015) Quantifying the impact of weak, strong, and super ties in scientific careers (PNAS)
finding: Defines super ties from the extreme tail of collaboration duration and paper overlap. Most ties are brief; a few are very strong and linked to higher output and citations (the apostle effect).
numbers: 473 researcher profiles (biology and physics), more than 166,000 collaboration records. 60-80% of ties last one year; 9% (biology) and 20% (physics) of researchers have a coauthor sharing over 50% of their papers; super-tie papers are about 52% of papers analysed.
quote: super ties contribute to above-average productivity and a 17% citation increase per publication
limits: Ego-network, correlational; selection of productive pairs possible. High-overlap coauthors may be students and advisors. Only pairs studied, not larger stable groups.
agent_relevance: A fixed complementary partner (a critic or verifier with a stable role) may beat a rotating set; no direct test in agents.

source: Petersen (2015) Quantifying the impact of weak, strong, and super ties in scientific careers (PNAS)
finding: Quantifies the super-tie benefit. Productivity effect is small; citation premium per paper is 17%. Note that 17% here is a citation boost, not team-size growth.
numbers: Productivity coefficient 0.11 +/- 0.01 (p<0.003), about 5.2% productivity gain when super ties give a third of coauthor input. Citation boost R = 1.17 (about 21 extra citations in biology, 8 in physics). Per-collaborator premiums: productivity about 8x, citations about 14x versus other coauthors.
limits: The SUBFIELDS row says team size grows about 17 percent per decade; that number was not found in this paper, which gives 17% as a citation premium. Flag the row for correction.
agent_relevance: Treat the row figure as unverified; do not cite 17% as a growth rate.

source: Petersen (2015) Quantifying the impact of weak, strong, and super ties in scientific careers (PNAS)
finding: Mechanisms offered: complementary skill sets, reward sharing, and reputation spillover from a high-status partner. Prior experience between the pair is associated with below-average productivity at fixed share.
numbers: Coefficient on prior-experience term negative (p<0.008 for all datasets except top biology). Share of papers that include a super tie: 54% (top biology), 45% (top physics), 74% (other biology), 54% (other physics).
limits: Mechanisms are interpretations, not tested separately.
agent_relevance: Stable pairing carries both value (complementarity) and a risk (staleness).

source: Milojevic (2014) Principles of scientific research team formation and evolution (PNAS)
finding: First model of team-size distribution. Two modes: small core teams from a Poisson process, and extended teams that grow by cumulative advantage on members' productivity, giving a power-law tail.
numbers: Astronomy: mean team size 1.5 in 1961-65 to 6.7 in 2006-10; 154,221 simulated articles; 90% of articles still have fewer than ten authors. Probability of publishing with an extended team held constant at 0.3 over 50 years; repeat-publication probability 0.8.
limits: A fit, not a causal test; assumes constant propensity. Tested on 6 fields only.
agent_relevance: Gives a growth mechanism for team size: preferential recruitment of productive members. Analogue: an agent pool that grows around the best-performing prompt or tool.

source: Milojevic (2014) Principles of scientific research team formation and evolution (PNAS)
finding: Analytic form fits many fields: two Poisson terms plus an exponentially truncated power law. Extended teams dominate at ten or more authors; standard core teams dominate up to eight.
numbers: Articles 2006-10: astronomy 31,473 (mean team 6.14), ecology 5,420 (3.54), mathematics 3,244 (1.93), social psychology 4,122 (2.93), literature 725 (1.05), arXiv 235,414 (3.36). KS D=0.05 to 0.17.
limits: Fits by KS test only; mathematics fit weakest (D=0.17). Literature too small for a test.
agent_relevance: Background; no direct agent claim.

source: Milojevic (2015) Quantifying the cognitive extent of science (J Informetrics)
finding: Bigger teams cover less cognitive territory, measured by lexical diversity of titles for equal quotas of articles.
numbers: 20 million articles in physics, astronomy and biomedicine. Papers by teams of 10 cover 85% of the maximum extent; about 60 members 60%; over 100 authors in physics 35%. In biomedicine extent peaks at teams of 3-5; solo authors lower.
quote: articles produced by larger teams cover significantly smaller cognitive territory than (the same quota of) articles from smaller teams
limits: Title vocabulary is a proxy for topic breadth; the metric is precise to under 1% but validity as a measure of ideas is indirect.
agent_relevance: Independent evidence that narrowing comes with scale, with a peak at small-but-not-solo size.

source: Lariviere, Sugimoto, Tsou, Gingras (2015) Team size matters: collaboration and scientific impact since 1900 (JASIST)
finding: Counter-direction to disruption: more authors, addresses and countries mean more citations, since 1900, and not just through self-citation.
numbers: 32.5 million papers and 515 million citations 1900-2011 (28.2M papers analysed). Sole-authored natural and medical papers fell from 87% (1900) to 7% (2011); social science and humanities 97% to 38%. Self-citation gain about 20% at 25 authors in SSH.
limits: Citation counts are correlational; larger teams self-promote. Does not measure novelty, so does not contradict Wu et al.
agent_relevance: Impact and novelty are different targets; pick the metric before choosing team size.

source: Lariviere, Sugimoto, Tsou, Gingras (2015) Team size matters: collaboration and scientific impact since 1900 (JASIST)
finding: Team-size inflation is long-run: authors per paper have to keep rising for papers to beat the world average citation rate.
numbers: Since the early 1980s, natural and medical papers with fewer than 21 authors saw falling mean relative citation rates; papers with 11-20 authors rose 2000% (0.22% to 4.5%) 1980-2011, papers with 21+ authors over 1000% (0.04% to 0.5%).
limits: Field-normalised citation rates by author count.
agent_relevance: Context for team-size growth; the true decadal growth rate still needs a source that was opened (open item).

source: Lin, Frey, Wu (2023) Remote collaboration fuses fewer breakthrough ideas (Nature 623)
finding: Remote teams are less disruptive than onsite ones across fields and team sizes. The gap tracks collaboration distance.
numbers: 20M papers (1960-2020) and 4M patents (1976-2020). P(D>0) falls 28% to 22% (papers, n=14,485,326) and 67% to 55% (patents, n=3,411,366) as distance goes from 0 km to over 400 km. Remote share of papers rose from 2% to 15% at intercontinental distance. Within-author remote penalty about 3-4% (20.4% to 19.5% for papers).
limits: Observational. Mostly citation-based disruption; mechanism inferred from contribution statements.
agent_relevance: Closest human analogue to separate agent contexts: less shared tacit knowledge means fewer integrated ideas.

source: Lin, Frey, Wu (2023) Remote collaboration fuses fewer breakthrough ideas (Nature 623)
finding: Remote work shifts roles: distant members join technical late-stage tasks, not conceiving or designing.
numbers: Probability two authors co-conceive research falls from 34% to 28% in remote teams. With four orders of magnitude citation gap, remote co-conceive probability falls from 33% to 23%. Same scientists switching onsite to remote: conceiving 63% to 51%, writing 60% to 49%, analysing 58% to 50%, performing 42% to 43% (n=21,373).
limits: Task labels from author contribution statements.
agent_relevance: Suggests keeping idea generation inside one shared context and farming out well-specified execution.

source: Holst et al. (2024) Dataset artefacts are the hidden drivers of the declining disruptiveness in science
finding: Contested replication of the disruption trend. The decline in CD index (Park et al. 2023) comes from records with zero references that were hidden from the plot but kept in the analysis.
numbers: 972,161 papers and 142,362 patents have CD5=1. In SciSciNet (39.9M papers) 97% of CD5=1 papers and 78% of such patents list zero references. Random citation behaviour also reproduces the decline.
limits: Targets the Park et al. time trend, not the team-size result directly; Wu et al. (2019) uses the same CD index, so artefact risk should be rechecked for team-size curves.
agent_relevance: Never trust a single citation metric; check data artefacts before using any disruption number.

source: Hao, Xu, Li, Evans (2024/2025) Artificial intelligence expands scientists' impact but contracts science's focus
finding: A language model was used to label AI-augmented papers; AI adopters gain personally while collective science narrows.
numbers: 41.3 million papers; classifier F1=0.875. AI users publish 3.02x more papers, get 4.84x more citations, lead projects 1.37 years (15.75%) earlier. Topics studied shrink 4.63%; follow-on engagement between scientists falls 22.00%.
limits: Observational; adoption confounded with career stage and field. Does not study team size directly.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as big teams: private gain, narrower shared focus. A warning for agent ensembles that converge on data-rich areas.

source: Bertalanic, Fortuna (2026) The Ringelmann effect in multi-agent LLM systems
finding: Scaling law for effective team size of LLM agents: R(N)=Neff/N=1/(1+c(N-1)N^-alpha), with hard-ceiling (alpha=0), sublinear and linear regimes. Dense debating agents are largely redundant.
numbers: 44 model-task-condition cells; Qwen, Llama, Ministral 7B-32B plus a Gemini check; fits R2>0.99. Thirty dense debating agents give no more answer diversity than one on MMLU-Hard. Asymptotic ceilings 1/c about 1.2, 1.8, 1.2 on three tasks. Fit on N<=5 predicts N=30.
quote: Thirty dense debating agents produce no more answer diversity than one on MMLU-Hard
limits: Preprint; open-weight models up to 32B; homogeneous teams. Authors name the Ringelmann effect as the analogy.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of diminishing returns to team size. Counted agents are not independent evidence.

source: Bertalanic, Fortuna (2026) The Ringelmann effect in multi-agent LLM systems
finding: Debate gain in homogeneous teams comes from re-evaluation, not peer content. Only architectural diversity lowers c and escapes the ceiling.
numbers: A noise placebo tracks self-correction on free-form math and at 4x scale. Qwen2.5-32B c=0.96 (MMLU-Hard), 0.77 (GSM-Hard), 0.97 (GPQA) versus 7B c=0.85, 0.57, 0.81. Communication-mode changes did not help.
limits: Within the tested configurations only.
agent_relevance: Supports using different models or personas, not more copies, and doubting self-debate as evidence.

source: Mieczkowski et al. (2026) Language model teams as distributed systems
finding: Distributed-systems lens on LLM teams: Amdahl's law bounds speedup, and teams fall short of the bound.
numbers: Highly parallel tasks gain most; ordering p0.9 > p0.5 > p0.2 (MWU p<0.001; Kruskal-Wallis H=61.4). Even highly parallel tasks stay below the Amdahl bound (Wilcoxon, median 2.19x, p<0.001); serial tasks gain nothing. Claude Sonnet 4.6 alone did not plateau significantly below the bound (p=0.45).
quote: Adding manpower to a late software project, makes it later.
limits: Simplified coding tasks with pre-assigned subtasks; token cost grows with team size (Spearman rho=0.40).
agent_relevance: Team size helps only the parallelisable share of a task; plan decomposition before spawning.

source: Mieczkowski et al. (2026) Language model teams as distributed systems
finding: Self-coordinating LLM teams show coordination cost: more messages and duplicated claims on tasks.
numbers: Self-coordinated teams send more messages than pre-assigned teams (Mann-Whitney U=311551, p<0.001), and counts rise with team size. Example: three Gemini agents all claimed the same task in round one.
limits: Qualitative examples are anecdotes.
agent_relevance: Needs a program-side assigner, as the schema already says: the program decides, the model fills slots.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a science of scaling agent systems
finding: Large controlled study of agent architectures. Multi-agent gains depend on task structure and saturate when the single agent is already good.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks, 5 architectures, 3 LLM families. Cross-validated R2=0.373 (0.413 with capability metric). Relative change vs single agent from +80.8% (decomposable finance) to -70.0% (sequential planning). Single-agent baseline above 45% gives negative returns (beta=-0.236, p=0.004). Picks the best architecture on 87% of held-out configurations.
limits: Moderate predictive power; frontier models only partly covered.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence: use a team only for decomposable tasks and when the lone agent is weak.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a science of scaling agent systems
finding: Error amplification differs by topology: independent agents amplify errors most; centralised verification contains them.
numbers: Trace-level error amplification: single 1.0, centralised 4.4, hybrid 5.1, decentralised 7.8, independent 17.2. Planning drops -39% to -70% for multi-agent variants.
limits: Error amplification main effect not significant after controls (beta=0.014, p=0.658).
agent_relevance: Argues for a central verifier (code check) over free peer voting.

source: Wuchty, Jones, Uzzi (2007) The increasing dominance of teams in production of knowledge (Science)
finding: Founding growth study of team authorship in science and engineering, social science and patents (recalled, not opened). Teams grew in dominance and gave more highly cited work than solo authors, with the gap widening over time.
numbers: Recalled and unverified: about 19.9 million papers and 2.1 million patents over five decades; mean team size in science and engineering rose from about 1.9 to 3.5. Check before use.
limits: Not opened this session; figures from memory.
agent_relevance: Cited by every later study here; the exact growth rate is what the SUBFIELDS row should be checked against.

source: Guimera, Uzzi, Spiro, Amaral (2005) Team assembly mechanisms determine collaboration network structure and team performance (Science)
finding: Model of team formation with parameters for team size, share of newcomers, and tendency to reuse past collaborators (recalled, not opened). Network structure and success follow from assembly rules.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Formal model for how teams are built; Milojevic (2014) notes it treats team size as a parameter.

source: Jones (2009) The burden of knowledge and the death of the Renaissance man (Rev Econ Stud)
finding: Economic explanation for team growth: knowledge accumulates, so each person specialises more and teams must be larger (recalled, not opened).
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Specialisation as a reason for teams, parallel to splitting a task by skill across agents.

source: Fortunato et al. (2018) Science of science (Science 359)
finding: Review that lists team science as one of six topics; source of the SUBFIELDS row framing (not opened).
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Background only.
